newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's ASEAN bid uncertain following fighting.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's ASEAN bid uncertain following fighting.

text.p: Political upheaval in Cambodia has cast the country's recent invitation to join the Association of South East Nations (ASEAN) into uncertainty, officials and analysts said on Monday.
Senior ASEAN officials planned to hold an emergency meeting on Saturday to discuss Cambodia's invitation to join ASEAN, Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said.
Cambodia, which was plunged into turmoil following two days of fighting in the capital Phnom Penh over the weekend, was to join ASEAN later this month along with Burma and Laos.

"If this fighting does not stop, obviously, ASEAN members will have to rethink this seriously...because they may not be capable of dealing with a situation of war inside the country," Siazon told reporters in Manila.

"The determination that has to be made at least in the scheduled special meeting of the senior officials (is) to determine whether the situation at that time, on Saturday, in Cambodia would require a reversal of the previous position.
"If the situation requires, we have to review the decision of the foreign ministers with respect to membership," Siazon said.
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen has taken control of Phnom Penh and its outskirts while his ousted rival Prince Norodom Ranariddh has vowed from France to organise resistance.
Indonesian Foreign Ministry spokesman Ghaffar Fadyl said ASEAN would soon release a statement on the Cambodia issue.
"We are now in consultations and very soon we will issue a joint foreign ministers' statement on the Cambodian issue," he told Reuters.
Informed sources said the statement was expected to express the regional group's concern over the fighting in the Cambodian capital.
Siazon said the text of a draft statement had been circulated among ASEAN members but was unsure when it would be finalised.
Siazon said ASEAN governments had been in touch with each other through Monday to discuss the Cambodia issue and that there had been a request for an emergency meeting of its foreign ministers.
He said ASEAN could possibly decide to delay the war-torn country's entry to the grouping while still admitting Burma and Laos.
The three countries were to join ASEAN's current seven members during a series of annual meetings to be held from July 22-28 in Kuala Lumpur.

"Although our leaders have taken a decision that all of the three will have to be accepted at the same time, I guess it would be possible," Siazon said, when asked if it was possible to delay Cambodia's entry.
Thai foreign minister Prachuab Chayasarn also said on Monday ASEAN may review its decision on accepting Cambodia during the annual meetings.

"The ASEAN meeting may consider reviewing its resolution of admitting Cambodia as a member of ASEAN but all this will depend on consultation (among ASEAN members) that will go on from today until the (late July) meeting date," Prachuab told reporters after a lunch with the ambassadors from ASEAN nations in Bangkok.

ASEAN has been involved in Cambodian affairs for almost the entire 30 years of its existence since the group was founded in 1967 at the height of the Vietnam war. ASEAN officials have said it was the country, not the government, that was being admitted to the seven-member grouping. ASEAN, which traditionally avoids intervening in domestic disputes, groups Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, Thailand, Singapore, the Philippines and Brunei.
Squeezed between Thailand and Vietnam with China as an interested party, Cambodia has strategic significance in the region, analysts said.

"Cambodia's interests are ASEAN's interests," Jusuf Wanandi, chairman of the supervisory board of Indonesia's Centre for Strategic and International studies, told an Asia-Pacific conference last month. Cambodia's membership in ASEAN could give it the security it needs to develop politically, he said.
ASEAN has long been involved in efforts to end Cambodia's three-decade long civil war and its seemingly insurmountable conflict between communist and royalist factions.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas played a key role in the Paris Peace accords that led to U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993 and the political chimera of a country ruled by two prime ministers who are sworn enemies.

The Paris accords were meant to end a civil war that began with the 1970 overthrow of the U.S.-backed Lon Nol government and descended into savagery with the 1975-79 "killing fields" regime of Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge.

Vietnam invaded in 1979 to oust Pol Pot and installed a pro-Hanoi regime under Hun Sen. ASEAN defined itself in the 1980s by opposing the Hun Sen government and supporting an anti-Vietnamese guerrilla coalition that included Ranariddh's royalists and the Khmer Rouge.

One Western diplomat said the international community would probably sit on the sidelines in the latest fracas, citing diplomatic fatigue with earlier peace-making efforts in Cambodia, which relies heavily on foreign aid.
